Ten years after creating its first movement, Chronométrie Ferdinand Berthoud unveils its new collection, “Mesure du Temps 1787”, whose principle is to reveal the mechanical beauty of the movement on the dial side.

A mechanical show staged on the dial side

Chapter 1 of this collection introduces the first model featuring this innovative architecture: the Chronomètre FB 2TV. Its Calibre FB‑TV.FC features a constant-force regulating device combining a tourbillon and a fusée-and-chain, while introducing a profoundly reimagined architecture after six years of research. Among its 1,240 components, enhanced by 300 hours of manual finishing, the 15 mm flying tourbillon, without an upper bridge, stands out and reinforces the movement’s visual impact.

Two complications dedicated to precision timekeeping

Two unprecedented complications enhance this movement. The first is a stop-seconds mechanism that allows the movement to be stopped for precise adjustment. The second is a flyback-type zero-resetting of the seconds hand, which can be activated by a coaxial pusher embedded in the dynamometric winding crown.

A thoroughly reengineered movement

The movement also benefits from significant optimisations: a new fusée geometry, a double stopwork system (upper and lower), a compact planetary differential system ensuring continuity of operation during winding, and a barrel equipped with a new pre-winding system. These developments ensure more constant torque, a power reserve extended to 60 hours, and faster winding.

A case and display designed to magnify the mechanism

From an aesthetic standpoint, the Chronomètre FB 2TV offers a harmonious three-dimensional architecture that showcases the mechanics. The off-centre display of hours and minutes, the central titanium seconds hand, and the power reserve indication via a mobile cone ensure both readability and technical coherence. The entire assembly is housed in a 44 mm white gold case.

Produced in a highly limited series (10 to 12 pieces per year), the Chronomètre FB 2TV thus embodies the convergence of traditional horological architecture, mechanical innovations dedicated to chronometry, and the sculptural highlighting of each component of the movement.

watches.name: Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges
specs:
Self-winding mechanical 
Power reserve: 55 h, 21600 vph 
Skeleton movement
watches.desc:
In 1867, Girard-Perregaux introduced the Three Bridges to the world. Transcending mere functionality by revealing the beauty of the movement, it became one of the oldest and most enduring design signatures in watchmaking. In 1975, the Maison launched the Laureato — the first and only fully in-house developed, designed, and crafted integrated-bracelet watch — an octagonal icon that celebrates its 50th anniversary this year. Yesterday, today and tomorrow now converge in a new icon – the Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges, a masterpiece uniting two legends, where craftsmanship and innovation become one. Two timeless signatures reunited.

For over 234 years, Girard-Perregaux has been shaping the history of design in watchmaking. Long before the word “design” entered the horological vocabulary, the Maison was already defining it. In 1867, Constant Girard revolutionized watch aesthetics by refusing to hide beauty behind a dial, proving that every technical element could also express emotion. He drew the arrow-shaped Three Bridges—a visionary composition where form and function became one.

Unlike the skeleton watches of the time, whose movements were adapted, the architecture of the Three Bridges was conceived as integral to the design itself, where structure became art, revealing what others chose to conceal. Over time, the design has evolved, but Constant Girard’s spirit still endures. Today, one of the oldest signatures in watchmaking takes on a contemporary expression while celebrating another icon: the Laureato.

Launched in 1975, the Laureato remains a fully in-house creation. Its harmonious play of geometric contrasts — an octagonal bezel, a circular ring, and a tonneau-shaped case — gives it a unique yet perfectly balanced identity.

Now, Girard-Perregaux unites two of its most enduring symbols in a single masterpiece: the Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges — where two legends converge into one timeless icon.

Technical mastery / Engineering in motion

The Girard-Perregaux philosophy allows the brand to achieve both visual openness and mechanical coherence, delivering remarkable torsional rigidity and impeccable symmetry.The Calibre GP9620, designed, developed and crafted in house specifically for the Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges, is structured around three white gold openworked bridges that form its visual and functional backbone. The upper bridge secures the barrel, beneath which the platinum micro-rotor is ingeniously positioned, the central bridge supports the gear train and motion works, and the lower one anchors the tourbillon. This alignment – barrel, gear train, and tourbillon on a single axis – remains a rare technical feat, both rational and poetic. This inverted construction – bringing components usually hidden at the back to the front – transforms the calibre into a living, mechanical sculpture.

At the base of the composition lies the tourbillon, a feature deeply rooted in Girard-Perregaux’s identity since Constant Girard’s pioneering 19th-century creations. Crafted in titanium, its iconic lyre-shaped cage combines lightness and strength to counter the effects of gravity on timekeeping accuracy, while a small seconds hand enhances functionality and rhythm. Every element of the Calibre GP9620 is designed for harmony: the gear train, bridges, and cage form a meticulously balanced geometry, ensuring visual equilibrium as well as optimal mechanical performance.

The platinum micro-rotor, placed behind the barrel, ensures automatic winding without interrupting the transparency of the design, silently converting the wearer’s natural wrist motion into stored energy. True to its architectural conception, the movement makes no compromise between form and function, delivering a power reserve of at least 55 hours. The baton-shaped hands, lined with luminescent material, glide above this technical landscape with serene clarity, guided by a minute track affixed to the inner case — a detail that enhances legibility without disturbing the purity of the skeletonised layout.

Aesthetic refinement / Beauty That Stops Time

In every creation, Girard-Perregaux turns technique into emotion, and the Laureato Three Gold Bridges is no exception. If the movement’s architecture defines its function, its finishing defines its soul. It reveals 418 hand-polished bevels, including 362 inward angles — a breathtaking technical and artistic achievement. Each internal corner, among the most challenging to polish, captures and reflects light in endlessly shifting ways, making the movement appear alive, breathing with brilliance. The arrow-shaped ends of the six bridges epitomize this mastery: their sharp, mirror-polished edges require hours of meticulous hand-finishing, expressing over two centuries of craftsmanship at the Manufacture.

The Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges breaks with convention by forgoing a traditional dial to reveal its full mechanical architecture. Suspended white-gold indexes float above the movement, glowing with a soft blue luminescence in low light — a modern touch that enhances both legibility and allure. At the base, a small arrow-shaped plate in white gold discreetly bears the initials of the master watchmaker who assembled and finished the piece — a quiet tribute to human expertise and the artistry behind each creation.

Visual harmony extends across the case and bracelet. White gold and steel compose a refined palette of light, each surface designed to reflect and sculpt it with precision. The 41 mm case, just 10.85 mm thick (11.25 mm for the diamond-set version), strikes a perfect balance between presence and elegance offering an optimal fit on the wrist — a testament to Girard-Perregaux’s mastery of proportions, even in a tourbillon timepiece. The edge of the octagonal white-gold bezel now features a newly defined polished bevel contrasting with a circular satin finish, creating a dynamic play of shapes that unites the octagon and circle — the essence of the Laureato.

The reworked case displays sharper lines, deeper bevels, and broader polished facets that catch light from every angle. The integrated steel bracelet flows seamlessly, its domed links adding movement and depth, while the triple folding clasp with octagonal pushers not only ensures comfort and aesthetic balance, but also integrates a ingenious tool-free fine-adjustment system that lets the bracelet extend by up to 4 mm in an instant. — a discreet yet thoughtful touch for perfect wearability.

Here, the geometry of the Laureato and the architecture of the Three Bridges speak the same language — precision, proportion, and timeless beauty. Sculpted from light itself, the Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges transcends time, expressing balance, heritage, and innovation in perfect harmony.

The Laureato Fifty Three Gold Bridges is limited to 50 pieces.

About Girard-Perregaux

A Manufacture of Design and a Manufacture of Movements since 1791. With over 30 calibres in its catalogue, 80 patents, and a legacy spanning more than 230 years, Girard-Perregaux is a master of Haute Horlogerie. From its origins, the brand stood out as a pioneer. In 1791, it introduced the idea of a modern integrated watch manufacture, the first of its kind, which would inspire the industry that followed. The founders and leaders of the brand, each in their time, advanced the prestige of the brand through their visionary and forward-thinking spirit. This spirit led to key milestones: the Three Bridges Tourbillon in 1867; the first ever high frequency mechanical movement in 1965, with a 36,000 vph; the universal quartz frequency (32,768 Hz) in 1971; and the Constant Escapement in 2013, winner of the Aiguille d’Or at the Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève. Each breakthrough is the result of an in-house team passionate about pushing boundaries while honoring tradition. Girard-Perregaux is also deeply design-driven. Every element - form, structure, aesthetics – is conceived, developed, and crafted in-house. The Tourbillon with Three Gold Bridges, awarded at the 1889 Paris Universal Exhibition, was revolutionary both technically and visually.

This philosophy found its purest expression in the Laureato. Launched in 1975 and entirely designed in-house, it draws inspiration from bold and symmetrical forms — a signature of Girard-Perregaux’s style — most notably expressed through its octagonal bezel, now a defining element of the Laureato’s visual DNA.

Over the years, the Laureato has embraced new complications and automatic movements, evolving while preserving its distinctive identity. Today, Girard-Perregaux is internationally respected and admired by watch lovers and collectors for its incomparable approach to Haute Horlogerie. It is a name synonymous with sophisticated luxury and timeless aesthetic… A Manufacture that has always remained true to its long and undeniable heritage.

Following the elegant and widely acclaimed design language of the Origine, Sylvain Pinaud introduces a new timepiece built on principles of balance, proportion, and clarity.

The architecture of the dial retains a refined asymmetry, carefully composed to preserve both visual harmony and legibility. The contrast between the black polished steel components, structuring the layout and the hand grained surfaces, plays with light in a unique way.

Particular attention has been given to proportions, resulting in a case and dial ensemble of notable coherence. The lines remain fluid and controlled, extending the neoclassical approach established by the Origine while introducing a stronger mechanical focal point.

As with all of Sylvain Pinaud’s creations, the movement is entirely developed and assembled in-house, with no compromise in terms of chronometry or reliability. The construction follows traditional watchmaking principles, using untreated or minimally altered materials such as nickel silver, titanium or gold, enhanced through extensive manual finishing.

The tourbillon’s 30-second rotation brings a constant, deliberate motion to the face of the watch, reinforcing the mechanical presence without overwhelming the overall composition. It is an invitation to dive into the mechanics and turn over the watch to discover the movement.

In the pursuit of chronometry, the tourbillon cage is made out of titanium in order to optimize efficiency with a 20% weight reduction, it offers an adequate balance between its inertia, and its fast rotation, and the movement frequency. A double barrel construction ensures stable energy delivery and a long power reserve.
In keeping with the chronometric mindset, the large seconds counter offer an aperture on the zero-reset mechanism, allowing for precise time-setting.

A particular attention was brought to the hand-finishing. Each component is hand-finished to the highest standards: bridges are bevelled with sharp inner angles, surfaces are either finely grained or satin finished, and steel parts are carefully brought to a black polish.
The large barrel bridge on the back is conceived as a sculptural element. The anglage work, hand-filed from a raw edge and hand polished, pays tribute to the finest traditions of watchmaking decoration through our own craftsmanship.
Wheels are individually decorated with anglage on both sides and circular brushing, and all functional elements are treated with the same level of attention, whether visible or not.

watches.name: Royal Oak "Jumbo" Extra-thin Selfwinding Flying Tourbillon Chronograph RD#5 "150th Anniversary"
specs:
Self-winding mechanical 
Power reserve: 72 h, 21600 vph

Hours, Minutes, Seconds, Flyback chronograph 
Flying Tourbillon
watches.desc:
Coinciding with Audemars Piguet's 150th anniversary, the brand unveiled the latest innovation from its Research & Development department. Combining technical sophistication, performance and iconic design with a new standard of ergonomic refinement, the Royal Oak “Jumbo” Extra-Thin Selfwinding Flying Tourbillon Chronograph RD#5 marks a new era in the history of chronographs and in the evolution of complications. Requiring five years of development by Audemars Piguet’s teams, this exceptional timepiece houses the all-new Calibre 8100, whose inner workings have been entirely reimagined and patented to meet the expectations of the most discerning collectors. Every detail has been meticulously crafted, pushing the boundaries of ergonomic design to redefine the touch-sensitivity of chronograph push-pieces. Notably, the RD#5 features a rare instant jump minute counter alongside an hour counter and – for the first time in the Royal Oak collection – combines a flyback chronograph with a flying tourbillon. Limited to 150 pieces, this milestone creation is crafted from titanium and precious bulk metallic glass (BMG) to offer a balance of lightness, durability and brilliance.

For over 150 years, chronographs have evolved in form and function, yet their core reset mechanism – based on the traditional hammer and heart piece – has remained largely unchanged. With Calibre 8100, presented for the first time in RD#5, Audemars Piguet has entirely reimagined the zero-resetting system, introducing an integrated flyback chronograph that is more ergonomic, intuitive, and precise. In-house engineers have developed a new, patented, mechanism that optimises energy from both the movement and the short-travel, low-force push-pieces. This innovation is based on a rack-and-pinion mechanism, designed to replace the conventional heart piece and hammer. By storing energy in the rack, this device keeps the gear train under tension and prevents the chronograph hand from shuddering while eliminating the need for the friction spring found in contemporary chronographs – a component acting as a constant break during operation and reset alike. The result is similar energy consumption, but the energy is now stored rather than dispersed.

Another challenge presented by traditional chronographs is the energy they require for resetting. To address this, the teams sought to develop a solution which would provide a smoother reset with reduced inertia. The energy stored in the rack can be released to return the chronograph hand to zero in a retrograde motion. By using titanium components, including the hand and chronograph wheel, the reset is instantaneous, requiring minimal energy.

The new Calibre 8100 not only features a flying tourbillon but also introduces an innovative vertical clutch system. This design combines traditional and friction clutches, allowing the clutch wheel to move vertically, which reduces unnecessary rotations and limits jumps. The calibre also features a column wheel that ensures smooth operation of the start and stop functions. For resetting, a patented system stores energy until it reaches a tipping point, then releases it all at once, ensuring the hands return to zero quickly and with precision*. On the back of the watch, Audemars Piguet's teams have developed a peripheral oscillating weight in platinum, reducing thickness and providing an unobstructed view of the movement's refined finishes, such as the hand-bevelled chronograph bridges, sharp inward angles, and satin finish. With a 72-hour power reserve, this robust chronograph easily adapts to modern lifestyles, including various sporting activities, without the risk of deregulating.


*Patent CN119325578A

With the Endeavour Flyback Chronograph Dual Time Date model, H. Moser & Cie. brings together a flyback chronograph, a second time zone and a date display in a composition of rare visual purity. No counters interrupt the harmony of the dial. The complications recede behind an instinctive, fluid reading of time. More than a traditional chronograph, the Endeavour Flyback Chronograph Dual Time Date evokes a precision instrument reinterpreted through the minimalist vision of H. Moser & Cie., a true invitation to travel. A complex watch that refuses to appear complicated, equipped with a new hand-wound movement developed by AGENHOR, partner of H. Moser & Cie.

The Endeavour Flyback Chronograph Dual Time Date model expresses a contemporary vision of travel: mobile, fluid and perfectly controlled. Its second time zone, subtly integrated at the centre of the dial, its tachometric scale inspired by measuring instruments, and its remarkably clean display come together in a watch designed for movement. A timepiece that crosses time zones with the same fluidity with which the eye moves across its dial. Sophisticated without ever being ostentatious, it is the ideal companion for the modern traveller.

Reinventing the traditional codes of the chronograph with the accent on space, balance and legibility, H. Moser & Cie. has chosen minimalism and restraint. All the indications are centralised to preserve the harmony of the dial, in two parts. The chronograph hands replace traditional counters, with the red hand indicating the seconds while the rhodium-plated hand displays the elapsed minutes.

The result is an immediacy: intuitive reading, free of any visual clutter. The second time zone also appears at the centre of the dial, on a fumé disc adorned with a discreet white arrow that blends naturally into the composition. True to the brand’s philosophy, the complication never seeks to dominate the aesthetic, instead dissolving into an exquisite clarity.

Developed with AGENHOR, the hand-wound HMC 730 calibre uses the retrograde principle to enable the elapsed minute hand to jump instantly using the energy accumulated and then released by a snail cam, it allows the values to be read with greater accuracy. It is equipped with a double barrel providing a 72-hour power reserve, displayed on the back of the movement to preserve the purity of the dial. The date can be adjusted both forwards and backwards without risk to the movement – a rare level of user convenience in such a sophisticated horological architecture.

watches.desc:
1816 was one of the great turning points in watchmaking history. It is the year in which the great watchmaker Louis Moinet completed the world's first chronograph.

This year, to celebrate the 210th anniversary of this invention, Les Ateliers Louis Moinet unveils a new edition of the 1816 CHRONOGRAPH in a warm champagne colour.

Reinventing heritage: The 1816 chronograph

A closer look at Louis Moinet’s new 1816 chronograph means taking a deep dive into over 200 years of history through a timepiece exhibiting a resolutely contemporary style. The DNA of the original timepiece, which with its sober, functional, and, for its time, avant-garde design, emerges in every detail. The aesthetic codes of the original model have been given a totally new interpretation but one that is always in keeping with the traditional codes of haute horlogerie.

A new edition for 210 years of the first chronograph

For this occasion, this new 1816 CHRONOGRAPH is adorned with a luminous champagne hue. This colour reflects the mechanics of the piece: an integrated, brand-new calibre engineered especially for this chronograph, which, naturally, evokes the mechanical tradition and haute horlogerie.

On the dial, this shade adds depth and warmth to the visual composition and creates a refined contrast with the blued steel hands. The rhodium-plated rings framing the counters give the design structure, which was inspired by the original timepiece, and enhance legibility.

The small seconds subdial and the 30-minute instantaneous totaliser, arranged horizontally on the top half of the dial on either side of the stationary central chronograph hand, overlook the 12-hour totaliser. The latter adopts Roman numerals for this edition, another nod to the original timepiece of 1816, while the upper sub-dials are distinguished by satin-brushed annular displays with Arabic numerals.

The entire dial is composed of twenty-three elements, including ten blackened nickel cabochons. The base and centres of the three champagne-coloured counters feature a bead-blasted finish. True to the original, the flange, which is divided into increments of six, is mounted onto the watch with four blued-steel screws.

Engraving has made it possible to precisely inscribe the dial markings, the name of the timepiece – 1816 – and the name Louis Moinet, reproduced in the typography of the original creation.

The central chronograph hand and the counters’ hands are made of heat-blued steel. The hours and minutes are indicated by Louis Moinet-style openworked hands, with tips coated in a luminescent substance.

The final touch is the fleur-de-lys logo at twelve o'clock. It pays homage to the city of Bourges, where Louis Moinet was born in 1768.

A louis moinet calibre in the finest watchmaking tradition

The challenge faced when designing the LM1816 calibre for the 1816 CHRONOGRAPH was to preserve the DNA of the original Louis Moinet chronograph while building a brand-new movement that would meet the standards of haute horlogerie. From the outset, the architecture of the movement was dictated by the unique position of the counters on the 1816 model.

The movement has 330 components, including 34 jewels, and runs at 28,800 vibrations per hour. The exhibition case back reveals the interplay of carefully finished parts, the overlapping planes and bridges, interweaving gears, and chronometric controls. The contrasts are striking: the white of the steel, the satin finish and brassy hue of the bridges, the blue of the fixing screws, and the deep red of the rubies.

Watch enthusiasts wishing to have a physical connection with their timepiece will appreciate the manual winding ritual, which ensures 48 hours of autonomy. The instantaneous minute counter, the column wheel control, and the swan-neck regulator are other elements that draw the expert eye, as they are hallmarks of authenticity, care and quality of the movement.

A distinctive case and a sculptural bracelet

The double-gadroon case, in polished and satin-finished grade 5 titanium, measures 40.6 millimetres in diameter and is composed of 51 parts. It retains its original Directoire style semi-bassine design with a smooth case middle. Two sober pushers frame the winding crown, which is decorated with a fleur-de-lys, the emblem of Bourges, Louis Moinet's birthplace. The elegant and timeless 1816 CHRONOGRAPH was made to be very comfortable on the wrist.

The champagne colour appears again on the intermediate links of the grade 5 titanium bracelet, which is integrated into the case. It highlights the distinctive U-shape of their architecture and accentuates the relief of this sculptural construction. The satin and polished finishes create a whole that is both fluid and ergonomic.

watches.desc:
At rest, the watch presents itself as a three-hand TONDA PF. Visual silence. Balance. Clarity. The dial reveals nothing and respects the hierarchy of civil time. The mono-pusher integrated into the caseband at 7.30 orchestrates the entire sequence. A single command. A single gesture coordinating three perfectly synchronised phases.

1. First press: deployment

The three rhodium-plated chronograph hands perform an instantaneous flyback. They position at 12 o’clock, start immediately and synchronise perfectly. From indicating civil time, they transform into chronograph measurement hands. At the same time, the rose gold hour and minute hands of civil time appear. The dual display organises itself seamlessly. Measurement unfolds across the full dial, freed from traditional sub-dials. The chronograph no longer exists at the periphery. It occupies the space entirely.

2. Second press: stop

The reading of measured time becomes immediately legible. The rhodium-plated hours, minutes and seconds hands indicate the measured time in relation to the rose gold civil time hands, without fragmentation or visual hierarchy.

3. Third press: withdrawal

The final gesture is not limited to a return to 12 o’clock. The rhodium-plated hands align precisely with the rose gold hands of current time, while the seconds hand resumes its natural motion. The complication disappears and the dial regains its original purity. A single hand performs the dual function of civil seconds and chronograph seconds. The complexity remains invisible. At Parmigiani Fleurier, discretion is not an aesthetic position. It is the result of mastery. This transition between appearance, presence and withdrawal defines the essence of the experience.

FOR ME, A WATCH IS A PERFORMANCE.

I created this watch with that same conviction.

Since the AK-01 in 2012, my quality standards have only grown sharper, shaped over time. This flyback chronograph is the result of a relentless pursuit of every detail: harmonious proportions, an aesthetic both balanced and bold, with generous hand-decorations.

Today, everything is born at the heart of our workshops. From the cases to the grand feu enamel dials, from the movement to the hand-stitched straps, every step passes through our hands. It is this freedom that gives the timepiece its character. This craftsmanship is refined every day; it evolves and is passed down through the generations.

DESCRIPTION

The RRCHF is the first Flyback Chronograph by REXHEP REXHEPI. It is powered by an entirely new movement, designed to combine technical innovation with aesthetic balance.
From the outset, the pursuit of slimness guided the entire project. Achieving such proportions required a complete rethinking of the movement’s architecture, making an integrated chronograph the only viable solution. The same level of care was devoted to every detail, from the movement’s construction and the case design to the precise height and curvature of the hands, as well as the dial’s aesthetics.

The grand feu enamel dial draws inspiration from vintage pocket-watch chronographs, while the hands feature downward-stepped tips, a detail that is aesthetical but also functional: it improves readability while allowing to fit the glass lower.

The RRCHF is equipped with a hand-wound calibre featuring a flyback chronograph and a jumping-minute counter. The movement is built around asymmetrical architecture, where each component is shaped not only for efficiency but also for visual harmony. Governed by a column wheel and lateral clutch, the chronograph adopts an unconventional layout. Through the caseback, only the chronograph elements are revealed, animating the mechanism and emphasizing its function.

Finishing : All components, visible and non-visible, are entirely hand-finished to the highest standards of quality and Genevan watchmaking tradition. The TAG Heuer Monaco Evergraph opens a new chapter in the Maison's enduring legacy of chronograph innovation. More than an evolution of the TAG Heuer Monaco, this timepiece embodies the second chapter of TAG Heuer's Avant-Garde Horlogerie and asserts a clear ambition: to reinvent the complication that has defined the Maison's DNA for over 160 years. Unveiled at Watches & Wonders 2026, the TAG Heuer Monaco Evergraph introduces user-centric innovation, designed to bring concrete value to the wearer: greater durability, enhanced reliability, and superior precision. It's not about innovating for the sake of difference, but about transforming the mechanical chronograph experience.

The design of this piece reinterprets the model's historical codes while projecting them into a contemporary version. Its 40mm square case in grade 5 titanium retains the silhouette of the original Heuer Monaco, while the left-sided crown harks back to the Calibre 11 of 1969. The elongated pushers, transparent dial, and suspended counters create an impression of depth and reveal the architecture of the movement. The taut lines, sharp facets, and refined profiles give the watch a presence that is at once technical, ergonomic, and almost architectural.

At the heart of this timepiece beats the Calibre TH80-00, developed around a compliant chronograph mechanism. After five years of research conducted by the TAG Heuer LAB, this system replaces traditional mechanical parts with two flexible bistable components: one dedicated to the start/stop functions, the other to resetting. This architecture reduces friction, improves operational consistency, and ensures a crisp, stable, and durable pusher feel. The Calibre also integrates the TH-Carbonspring oscillator, another TAG Heuer innovation resulting from nine years of R&D: extremely lightweight, shock-resistant, and anti-magnetic, it offers superior chronometric stability and accuracy. With a total of seven patents, an inverted movement construction, a frequency of 5 Hertz, a 70-hour power reserve, and a COSC certification, the Calibre TH80-00 positions the TAG Heuer Monaco Evergraph beyond mere evolution: it's a true revolution in mechanical chronography.

Marking a century and a half of horological excellence, Audemars Piguet is pleased to unveil the 150 Heritage pocket watch – a creation that celebrates the history of humankind, bridging centuries of astronomical observation, technical mastery and craftsmanship. At its heart beats Calibre 1150, the new ultra-complicated movement that builds on the core architecture of Calibre 1000, with all activation mechanisms – such as crown-pushers and correctors – entirely reimagined to suit the compact pocket watch format and its intended use. This limited edition also introduces the Universal Calendar for the first time: a mechanical calculator visible from the caseback and independent of the movement, offering a panoramic view of the celestial cycles that have shaped cultural celebrations across the world. With 47 functions, including 30 complications*, the 150 Heritage harmoniously blends complications with intuitive operation, reflecting the brand’s commitment to putting ease of use at the centre of mechanical innovation. Showcasing an array of métiers d’art, this pocket watch is adorned with hand-engraved platinum, luminous ‘Grand Feu’ enamelling and a hand-made chain, each element celebrating the traditional crafts that characterise Haute Horlogerie. The first ultra-complicated watch truly designed to fit inside a pocket, it lays the foundation for a new horological concept that blends tradition, innovation and modern portability.

Housed in the pocket watch’s caseback cover, the Universal Calendar draws inspiration from humanity’s relationship with the sky. Unlike traditional perpetual calendars, which follow a single time system, this mechanism embraces the plurality of interpretations around the world. Its dial not only presents complex astronomical data but also offers an alternative way to experience time by blending horology with astronomy and tradition. the Universal Calendar itself compiles 8 complications which bring together solar, lunar and lunisolar cycles on a single dial for a 360° panorama counting 18 indications: the year, leap years, months, dates, weeks, moon phase and seasonal markers, such as solstices and equinoxes, and nine cultural celebrations drawn from global traditions. Some celebrations are based on the Sun – Christmas (Sol Invictus) and Saint John’s Day (Inti Raymi); some on the Moon – the beginning of Ramadan; and others are lunisolar, including Diwali, Rosh Hashanah, Pesach, Vesak, Easter and the Chinese New Year. Each event is shown as a consequence of an astronomical phenomenon, creating a strong connection between the cosmos and human tradition.

BOVET Presents the Récital 31 – A New Chapter in the Perpetual Calendar

BOVET unveils the Récital 31, a new interpretation of the perpetual calendar that combines high horology, celestial complexity, contemporary wearability, and greater ease of use.

Inspired by owner Pascal Raffy’s enduring fascination with the movement of celestial bodies and the precision of calendar watchmaking, the Récital 31 rethinks one of horology’s most demanding complications.

Fleurier, Switzerland — BOVET is proud to introduce the Récital 31, a bold new chapter in the Maison’s Récital collection and a refined expression of its commitment to exceptional watchmaking. Long associated with high complications, BOVET continues to evolve its creative language, producing timepieces designed to make watchmaking’s most sophisticated mechanisms more intuitive for collectors to wear, enjoy, and feel every second.

The perpetual calendar is one of the most complex and functional complications in haute horlogerie, capable of accounting for the varying lengths of months and leap years over decades. With the Récital 31, BOVET brings this technical mastery into a 44 mm Dimier case with a box sapphire crystal, creating a timepiece that is both highly expressive and eminently wearable.

To address a constant complaint of collectors, the corrector pushers for the perpetual calendar and the moon phase are clearly labeled and engraved on the case itself. No more guessing and adjusting the wrong indication. In doing so, the Maison delivers a more intuitive experience without compromising the sophistication of the movement.

Pascal Raffy’s Vision

“I have always been fascinated by perpetual calendars; it is one of the most beautiful complications in watchmaking history,” explains Mr. Raffy. “I wanted to develop a 100% in‑house movement with a spherical moon phase and a clear, intuitive display for all the indications, so that this complication could become truly practical for everyday use. We continue to defend art, beautiful guilloché, and hand‑engraving. The Récital 31 is a substantial timepiece, designed with both poetry and precision in mind.”

The Récital 31 continues the design evolution initiated by the Récital 30, in whose design Mr. Raffy’s children – Audrey, Alexandra, and Amadéo – were instrumental, further advancing BOVET’s vision of a wearable high complication. It represents a fresh and modern interpretation of the perpetual calendar, one that preserves the romance and intellectual depth of traditional watchmaking while responding to the needs of today’s collector.

New Manufacture Movement

At the heart of the timepiece lies a new in-house movement featuring a perpetual calendar, a spherical precision moon phase, hand-engraved finishing, and the artisanal decoration for which BOVET is known. Combining the moon phase with the perpetual calendar with retrograde date was a challenge for BOVET’s technical office, due to space and available power restrictions. BOVET has included moon phases with perpetual calendars in previous Grand Complications, like the GPHG highest award-winning Récital 22 Grand Récital, and with annual calendars like in the Récital 20 Astérium, which won the Calendar and Astronomy Award at the GPHG. This is, however, the first time this celestial indication has been paired with a perpetual calendar alone.

Mr. Raffy’s commitment is to do as many processes in BOVET’s own facilities as possible. Since 2006, when he acquired the manufacture in Tramelan, BOVET has increased its in-house production capabilities, with more than 95% of all components now done in Tramelan. This level of true mastery has not gone unnoticed, with more than 70 awards in the 20 years since, and 6 GPHG awards in the last 8 years.

The 469-component movement is exquisitely hand-finished and hand-engraved. A new engraving motif was developed for the Récital 31 and the Récital 32, named étoiles carrées or “square stars.” The engraving of the movement alone takes more than 15 hours in BOVET’s in-house atelier. This level of attention to detail reflects BOVET’s focus on the human touch – no assembly lines can be found anywhere in the manufacture or castle.

Available in titanium or 18K red gold, the Récital 31 reflects a balance of technical rigor, aesthetic refinement, and contemporary comfort. This year, the Récital 31 is available in three color combinations, with rubber straps matching the dial color, and each variation is limited to 60 numbered pieces.

With the Récital 31, BOVET once again confirms its ability to unite technical invention, artistic craftsmanship, and everyday usability in a single creation. The result is a timepiece that feels both timeless and ahead of its time, reinforcing the Maison’s position at the forefront of contemporary haute horlogerie.

Récital 31 At a Glance

  • Perpetual calendar with retrograde date, with clearly labeled corrector pushers for date, day, month, and precision spherical moon phase
  • Brand new 469-component manufacture movement with 5 days of power reserve
  • 100% inhouse manufacture movement
  • 44mm x 13.3mm Dimier case with a box sapphire crystal
  • Exquisitely hand engraved movement featuring the new étoiles carrées “square stars” motif
  • Available in grade 5 Titanium or 18K red gold
  • Three color combinations offered – Blue, Red, and Black, each limited to 60 numbered pieces

Seen from Earth, Venus is, after the Sun and the Moon, the clearest object in the sky and has about the same size, mass and composition as earth. Nevertheless, living on the planet Venus is impossible as the average temperature is 462 degrees Celcius (864°F) and its atmospheric pressure is 90 times more than that of planet earth.

The new Venus is equipped with the - in 2024 introduced - CKM-01 movement, with the newly developed, extremely sophisticated, astronomical Venus module. The dial consists of 4 separate discs, of which 3 discs are rotating and carrying the celestial bodies, Venus, Earth and Moon.

The dials shows a planetarium, a part of our solar system. The real-time position and orbits of the planet Venus and planet earth around the sun as well as the position and the orbit of the moon around planet earth

The Venus Annual Calendar is a more technical interpretation of the Venus models and carries its celestial bodies on white, almost matt dial. On the outside ring, the Annual Calendar shows the days of the month in black and white rail track, housed in sections of each month, indicating the length of that month.

Because of this scaled print of the date-track, the Venus Annual Calendar needs only one correction every 4 years, the corrections can be done very conveniently via the crown.

On the discs that carry the planets you can find particular information, like Earth’s orbit time around the sun that takes 365.2 days. The orbital speed of the Earth around the Sun is a mind boggling 107’206 Km per hour, that of Venus is even faster at 126’071 Km per hour.

The time that Venus needs to make one full orbit around the Sun is 224.7 days. This astronomical masterpiece shows the phases of the moon in an unusual and innovative manner. If the Moon is exactly between the Sun and the Earth, it is a ‘new Moon’. If the Earth is between the Moon and the Sun, it is a ‘full Moon’.

And why do we have this complication, and the name ‘Venus’? Because it is based on the ‘old’ Venus from approx. 2006. That watch also showed the orbit of Venus and Earth around the Sun, while the Moon is orbiting Earth with its own orbital time. Back in the day, the watch was based on an ETA movement, with the wonderful module made by Mr. van der Klaauw.

Nowadays it houses our own beautiful movement (CVDK CKM-01 movement) with star-shaped bridges, beveled by hand and rhodium plated. And the skeletonized rose gold-plated brass rotor, shaped into the CVDK logo.

The CKM-01 movement in the Venus is the same as in the Planetarium, Real Moon Joure and Grand Planetarium from 2024 and newer.

The Krayon Anyday Rose Gold reimagines the calendar display through a new in-house complication designed to make reading the date and day both immediate and intuitive. Created for everyday use, the Anyday serves as an instantly legible agenda on the wrist, bringing clarity and simplicity to the passage of time.

“Would you be free for a coffee on the 10th?” A single glance at the wrist is enough. From this idea, the Anyday was born, making the calendar as intuitive to read as the time itself.

This creation is housed in a 39 mm rose gold case, highlighting a central anthracite grey dial with a sunray finish, adorned with the signature “Y” guilloché of the Krayon manufacture.

The central dial is surrounded by a sapphire disc graduated from 1 to 31, dedicated to the display of the simple date. The moon crescent advances day by day around the dial and performs an instantaneous jump at midnight to indicate the next date.

The distinction between weekdays and weekends is achieved through the colours of a painted disc located beneath the date disc. Depending on the date displayed, anthracite segments indicate weekdays, while golden segments indicate weekends.

Between the 31st and the 1st, four dots positioned at 6 o’clock extend the display and allow the first four days of the following month to be visualised.

Comprising 378 components, the Anyday requires only five manual adjustments per year. All settings are made directly via the crown: in the first position, a clockwise rotation adjusts the date, while a counterclockwise rotation adjusts the day of the week. The second crown position is reserved for setting the time.

Finally, the case back highlights the Krayon Waves present on the bridges, whose curves translate throughout the year the sunset function in Neuchâtel. In greater detail, one edge of the barrel bridge follows the shoreline of Lake Neuchâtel, the home territory of the Krayon manufacture.

Parmigiani Fleurier approaches this complexity with restraint. A coaxial display architecture preserves the purity of the dial, with two sub-dials at 4 and 8 o’clock concentrating the information: Day and Date on the first, Months and Leap Years on the second.

The dial, crafted in 18-carat rose gold, appears in the refined shade of Bright Peony with a hand-hammered finish. Inside beats the CALIBER PF733, operating at 4 Hz with a 60-hour power reserve. The movement reveals rose gold bridges decorated with hand-guilloché Clou de Paris and Filet sauté.

The new creative collaboration between Karl-Friedrich Scheufele (Chopard Co-President), the Chopard design team, Andrea Michele Zagato (Zagato President) and Norihiko Harada (Zagato Chief Designer) combines iconic codes from both Maisons to introduce a true concept watch showcasing the watchmaking prowess of the Manufacture's workshops founded in Fleurier in 1996 with the avant-garde spirit of the Italian coachbuilder. Today, the Zagato Lab One Concept model is a horological tribute to the automotive designer.

Ceramicised titanium: properties tried and tested in automotive construction

The 42 mm diameter case along with the movement bridges and mainplate are made from ceramicised titanium. This ultra-resistant metal is obtained by a process of oxidising titanium through electro-plasma technology: a treatment endowing it with a hardness of 1000 Vickers as well as shock and scratch resistance comparable to that of ceramic. A material developed for use in aerospace and automobile construction, ceramicised titanium also features an anthracite grey colour that does not fade over time – a welcome feature in a watch designed for the most extreme conditions.

This year, Grand Seiko is proud to present the Spring Drive U.F.A. Ushio 300 Diver, the brand’s first diver’s watch equipped with a U.F.A. movement, offering an exceptional accuracy of ±20 seconds per year. Ever since its first watch in 1960, Grand Seiko has always striven to create the best watches possible. Because a diver’s watch demands uncompromising performance, from precision to water resistance, creating one powered by the U.F.A. movement was the natural next step in Grand Seiko’s ongoing pursuit of excellence. The result is Grand Seiko’s smallest diver’s watch ever, and its most accurate to be powered by a Spring Drive movement.

Spring Drive U.F.A.

In 2025, Grand Seiko unveiled a groundbreaking Spring Drive movement, Caliber 9RB2. With a maximum yearly deviation of ±20 seconds, it is unquestionably the most accurate mainspring-powered wristwatch movement in history*, which is why we named it Ultra Fine Accuracy, or “U.F.A.” Powering the Ushio 300 Diver is Caliber 9RB1, a U.F.A. movement specially adapted for enhanced robustness to meet the demands of diving while maintaining the exceptional annual accuracy of ±20 seconds.

A timeless source of inspiration in Japan’s art and culture

The new creation strikes a perfect balance between function and beauty. The watch showcases a blue variation of the “Ushio” dial, a design theme that has been part of the Grand Seiko diver’s watch since 2022. The term ushio, which means “tide” in Japanese, evokes the waters that surround the Japanese archipelago, a timeless source of inspiration in the country’s art and culture. Combined with a gradient design, the vivid dial color emphasizes the dial pattern while ensuring the excellent legibility for which Grand Seiko diver’s watches are renowned.

Evolution 9 Collection

This diver’s watch belongs to the Evolution 9 Collection, which is guided by Grand Seiko’s design philosophy, the Evolution 9 Style. While preserving and honoring the original Grand Seiko design code, the Evolution 9 Style elevates this design language to new heights by focusing on three key pillars: aesthetics, legibility, and wearing comfort.

watches.desc:
In the late 1980s, Reebok introduced the Pump sneaker, quickly becoming an icon for an entire generation. More than just a sneaker, the Pump was an attitude, a statement that performance could go hand in hand with pleasure. And above all, it was a gesture that became cult: a simple press to connect with the shoe, adjust it, personalise it, and feel it come alive. H. Moser & Cie. shares with Reebok the conviction that luxury is at its best when it does not take itself too seriously. It is this playful sophistication that the two brands set out to celebrate by transposing the Pump gesture into watchmaking.

As Reebok prepares the return of the Pump in 2026, H. Moser & Cie. imagined an unexpected bridge: winding a mechanical movement using the iconic orange button. The reference is obvious, but the execution is delightfully precise. Replacing the traditional crown, an anodised aluminium pusher transmits the energy of each press to the barrel spring, simultaneously activating the power reserve indicator. An ingenious mechanical choreography unfolds beneath the surface, visible through openworked bridges and a fully skeletonised rack.

One simple press is enough for more than one hour of power reserve. And once the spring is fully charged, there is no need to stop: the button can still be pressed, purely for pleasure. Because some gestures need no justification.

To create this new calibre, H. Moser & Cie. completely re-engineered its automatic HMC 500 movement with the micro-rotor, transforming it into a manual-winding calibre. Compact and remarkably slim, it lent itself naturally to this ambitious technical reinterpretation, in which every component finds its place with precision. The sapphire case-back reveals the result: a sharpened, lightweight engine designed to accommodate the Pump system while preserving the brand’s minimalist DNA.

The Streamliner Pump is offered in two versions, each limited to 250 pieces. Its case is crafted from a material rarely seen in watchmaking: forged quartz fibre. Purer and whiter than glass fibre and resistant to UV exposure, quartz fibre can be coloured, offering a level of aesthetic freedom that carbon does not allow. Cut into segments, placed in a mould and compressed, it is combined with injected resin before undergoing two successive curing cycles. This process gives rise to matte cases with a unique moiré pattern — no two are alike. Inside, an internal titanium “sarcophagus” acts as a protective exoskeleton: it shields the movement, ensures water resistance to 10 ATM, and secures the integrated rubber strap.

On the wrist, the watch measures 11.4 mm in thickness, a confident presence made surprisingly light thanks to the quartz fibre and to the titanium elements, such as the sarcophagus and the caseback, this one finished with a DLC coating on the darker version. watches.desc:
Limited to 250 pieces, the Big Pilot’s Watch Perpetual Calendar Ceralume® features a 46.5-millimetre case crafted from luminous white ceramic. IWC’s proprietary luminous ceramic marks the latest chapter in the brand’s pioneering work with this material and was developed by its in-house engineering division XPL in collaboration with Super-LumiNova® specialists RC Tritec. To create it, ceramic powders and Super-LumiNova® pigments are homogeneously blended through a dedicated ball-milling process. These photoluminescent pigments behave like a light-storage battery: they absorb energy from sunlight or artificial light, store it temporarily, and release it in the dark as a vivid blue glow that lasts for more than 24 hours. The white dial and white rubber strap are likewise enriched with Super-LumiNova® pigments, further intensifying the luminous effect.

In daylight, the watch plays with contrasting shades of white and grey and an interplay of matte and shiny surfaces. In darkness, the case, dial and strap radiate an intense blue light, while the numerals and the edges of the hands appear as dark shadows against the glowing dial. The luminous effect extends all the way to the case back: the “Probus Scafusia” medallion integrated into the rotor is also crafted from luminous material. The case back ring and crown are crafted from stainless steel, creating a striking contrast with the ceramic case.

At the heart of the watch is IWC Schaffhausen’s legendary perpetual calendar, originally developed by Kurt Klaus in the 1980s. The calendar is mechanically programmed to recognize the varying lengths of every month and automatically adds a leap day at the end of February every four years. The date, weekday, month and moon phase are displayed across four subdials, while a four-digit year display is located between 7 and 8 o’clock. The signature Double Moon® display shows the moon phase as seen from both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, deviating by just one day every 577.5 years.

Driving this Big Pilot’s Watch is the IWC-manufactured 52616 calibre. Featuring a Pellaton automatic winding system reinforced with virtually wear-free ceramic components, the movement delivers a power reserve of 168 hours (7 days) and is visible through the sapphire glass case back.

Chopard’s latest creation takes the form of an extraordinary pendant watch, conceived as a precious walnut. Entirely crafted in-house, this singular piece showcases the Maison’s mastery of both jewellery and watchmaking, while continuing the creative legacy of the Animal World collection imagined by Caroline Scheufele – Chopard’s Co-President and Artistic Director.

This mysterious walnut is crafted in 18-carat ethical rose gold set with brown and cognac diamonds, then finished with a patina that lends the creation striking realism. A bespoke hidden hinge, released by a cognac diamond, allows the walnut to open, revealing a moonphase watch powered by an in-house self-winding movement. Displaying the hours, minutes and moonphase, the dial is framed by blued titanium and diamonds, with a sapphire-set crown positioned at 12 o’clock. An integrated sliding mechanism enables the display to be angled for optimal legibility, while the moonphase corrector remains discreetly concealed. When deployed, the display reveals the word “PEACE” engraved on both sides, expressing the creation’s central message.

The opposite half-shell presents a three-dimensional jewelled scene. Against a backdrop of blued guilloché titanium, a diamond-set dove carrying an olive branch takes flight, surrounded by diamonds that appear to float in space thanks to an ingenious setting technique. Fine diamond guipure, a signature of Chopard’s jewellery savoir-faire, creates a lace-like effect around the composition, while heart motifs subtly reference one of the Maison’s most cherished symbols, reinforcing a message of peace, hope and harmony.

The pendant watch is presented on a sumptuous sautoir crafted in 18-carat ethical rose gold, set with nearly 430 carats of brown, cognac and yellow briolette-cut diamonds cascading in a richly textured composition, reminiscent of tree bark.

watches.desc:
In celebration of the Maison’s 40th anniversary, Jacob & Co. introduces the Angel Cut, a diamond cut of its own invention. Patented and refined in-house over two years, it makes its debut in the Billionaire Double Tourbillon.

The Angel Cut solves a long-standing problem in gem cutting. Rectangular stones preserve more of the rough than round brilliants, but return light less vividly. Rather than add facets, Jacob & Co. reworked the geometry. The cut has 37 facets, fewer than most traditional cuts, arranged around a lozenge-shaped table within a stepped rectangular outline with cut corners. Calibrated crown height, pavilion depth, and facet alignment send light upward in a continuous glow rather than scattered flashes. The effect is a brilliance that feels composed: bright without harshness, fiery without fragmentation, and alive even in the low light inside a gem-set case. The 37 facets carry a second meaning: they mark the 37 years of marriage between Jacob Arabo and his wife Angela, after whom the cut is named.

The watch is built to showcase the cut at scale. Its 54 × 41 mm white-gold case is set with 98 Angel Cut diamonds totaling 51.13 carats, many of them unusually large, while the crown is set with a rose-cut white diamond. The dial adds 88 more, invisibly set and framing the twin tourbillon apertures. The inner rings of the double tourbillons are further adorned with 80 white diamonds, while the folding clasp is invisibly set with an additional 30 Angel Cut diamonds. Altogether, the watch is set with 297 diamonds totaling approximately 80 carats.

Beneath the diamonds, the hand-wound JCAM50 calibre comprises 460 components and offers a 72-hour power reserve. Its two flying tourbillons, positioned at 12 and 6 o’clock and linked by a differential, animate the openworked movement while averaging their rates through a shared regulating system. Visible through the sapphire caseback, the skeletonized architecture allows light to pass through the movement, reinforcing the transparency and brilliance of the Angel Cut diamonds.

Limited to 6 pieces.

Black opal has always been dear to Piaget - As Yves Piaget said, “The world is like an opal made of different tastes and sensibilities.” Just as there are no two opals alike, there are no two wearers of Piaget alike.

Self-winding mechanical 
Power reserve: 40 h, 21600 vph
watches.desc:
Celestial Voyager VK Edition

A platinum world time watch capturing the poetry of 14 cities around the world.

Introduction

ANDERSEN Genève presents the Celestial Voyager VK Edition. Created in collaboration with prominent New York–based private collector Vasu Kulkarni, this extraordinary project encompasses a limited edition of fourteen unique timepieces (one for him, twelve for his friends, plus one artist proof)—believed to be the first time a single cohesive series of world-timer watches has been commissioned with fourteen entirely distinct miniature-painted dials, each depicting a different city.

Each watch features a unique miniature-painted dial highlighting the city where its owner resides or holds a deep connection: New York, Greeley, Los Angeles, Toronto, Sydney, Taipei, Tokyo, New Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Prague, Madrid, and Zürich. Each dial composition was personally directed by Kulkarni, who worked closely with his friends to select landmarks, define spatial relationships, and ensure each city's unique character was faithfully captured in miniature.

The inaugural Celestial Voyager VK Edition showcases the scenery of New York City, with a dial that captures the beauty and energy of the city that never sleeps. At its centre, a micro-painted depiction of the New York City skyline at sunset is rendered in stunning detail directly onto a disc of dark Tahitian mother-of-pearl, in a space less than 2cm in diameter. Around the skyline, the iridescent nacre serves as both the luminous sky and the shimmering surface of the East River—a kaleidoscopic sunset ambience that shifts dynamically with the light.

Background

Over the past four decades, ANDERSEN Genève has emerged as the leading authority in highly crafted worldtime watches made in the classical tradition of Louis Cottier, the complication’s inventor. This expertise traces back to founder Svend Andersen’s work with Cottier-derived world timers in Patek Philippe’s Grand Complications workshop during the 1970s. Through successive series and innovations, the elegant worldtime complication has become a cornerstone of the ANDERSEN Genève watchmaking. It uses a sophisticated, ultra-slim in-house module first designed by Svend in 1989, which has been repeatedly refined over the years.

First launched in 2021, the Celestial Voyager was conceived as the ultimate expression of the worldtimer with a decorative dial, a highly coveted format in haute horlogerie. Notable for its classical dual-crown construction and distinctive “eagle’s wing” lug design, it has since become a canvas for bespoke unique pieces and ultra-limited editions that showcase Swiss artisan craftsmanship in its most exquisite forms, from grand feu and cloisonné enamel to mother-of-pearl, guilloché and 21ct BlueGold.

Previous editions include two “Sunset over Cappadocia” versions, the “Aurora/Arctic Sunrise Borealis”, “Sakura” editions, and the “Supersonic”, which celebrated Concorde soaring over New York City.

Celestial Voyager VK Edition: A UNIQUE EXPRESSION OF 14 cities around the world

The Celestial Voyager VK Edition distils the romance of 14 different cities into 14 unique timepieces, beginning with New York. Never before has a single commission yielded such a breadth of miniature-painted cityscapes within one unified collection—each dial a self-contained work of art, yet all sharing the same horological DNA and artistic vocabulary.

At its heart, a luminous dark Tahitian mother-of-pearl dial frames a hand-painted miniature of the Manhattan skyline. A light blue mother-of-pearl city ring encircles a 24-hour aventurine ring divided for day and night: blue aventurine by night, and aventurine overlaid with mother-of-pearl by day, with raised golden numerals standing in relief against the background.

The city ring is set in mother-of-pearl with blue lettering, with New York picked out in gold and the customary Andersen “A” at the Geneva position. Each of the 14 timepieces will have its depicted city highlighted in gold.

Skeletonised leaf-shaped hands in brushed yellow gold, a Celestial Voyager signature, complete the face. A subtle, highly personal reference to the city of the championship-winning Knicks is found on the 9 o'clock crown—used for setting the city ring—which bears a basketball motif, a nod to Kulkarni's passion for the sport.

THE ART OF miniature-PAINTING

The central scene depicts Manhattan as viewed from Brooklyn. The Brooklyn Bridge spans the East River in the foreground; beyond it lies the Seaport shoreline, with the Empire State Building standing tall at the centre, alongside One World Trade Center, the Chrysler Building and Rockefeller Center. All this is depicted in a space of just 18.3mm in diameter.

To capture it, ANDERSEN Genève worked with master artisans to develop a rarely-seen technique of miniature-painting directly onto dark Tahitian mother-of-pearl. Working with specialised acrylic paints and lacquers applied on both sides of the disc, layer upon layer of colour is built up to create an almost sculptural, three-dimensional effect against the shimmering background, where purples, pinks and yellows dazzle to form a unique New York sunset. To further elevate the artistry, fine gold cloisonné-style trim outlines the architectural elements, giving the miniature painting an authentic, raised enamel appearance that evokes the grand tradition of Swiss cloisonné work.

For the finest details, the artist uses brushes with as few as one to three hairs. This enables extraordinary details like brickwork and suspended cables of the historic Brooklyn Bridge, the reflective sheen of the One World Trade Center tower, the curving segments of the Chrysler Building spire and the uniform windows of the skyscrapers to be rendered with microscopic detail. Each dial takes a minimum of two weeks to complete; any mistake bears the risk of the artist having to start over.

Across the fourteen dials, the dark Tahitian mother-of-pearl is deliberately left unpainted in areas representing sky and water, allowing the nacre's natural peacock iridescence—its shifting greens, purples, and blues—to become an integral part of each composition. No two discs are alike; the organic variations in the mother-of-pearl ensure that every dial possesses a unique luminosity that no paint could replicate.

ARTISAN HOROLOGY, ANDERSEN GENÈVE-STYLE

The refined 37.8mm case is crafted in Pt 950 platinum and carries the distinctive “eagle’s wings” lugs, a hallmark of the Celestial Voyager line. Each lug has a curving, pointed form with a scooped-out, convex profile that maximises light reflection — exceedingly difficult to polish and time-consuming to make in any metal, and exceptionally so in platinum. Each lug is then individually soldered to the body of the case, a traditional method rarely found in modern watchmaking. The polished bezel and lugs contrast strikingly with the horizontally brushed finish of the case body, which is also carried out by hand.

The watch’s two symmetrical crowns echo the ancestry of the third ANDERSEN Genève worldtime watch: the “Mundus” (made in 1995 and still today the thinnest ever worldtime watch!). They are extremely thin in the pursuit of elegance, yet still tactile given their width. The left crown, that bears a the basketball motif, adjusts the city ring, while the right crown, engraved with the ANDERSEN logo (A), adjusts the time.

On the reverse, the artistry continues. The ring around the movement is also fashioned from turquoise mother-of-pearl, while the winding rotor is made of 21-carat BlueGold, heated to a rich shade of deep blue and decorated with an intricate, interlocking wave-form hand guilloché.

21ct BlueGold is an ANDERSEN Genève speciality, created by heat-tempering 24ct gold mixed with iron elements to achieve radiant shades – a jewellery-making technique that, in watches, ANDERSEN Genève alone has mastered.

The slimline movement exhibits a wealth of hand-finishing — chamfering, Geneva stripes, snailed wheels, mirror-polished screws and even polished crown-wheel teeth. All components are 100% Swiss-made, in the ANDERSEN Genève ateliers in Geneva and La Chaux-de-Fonds or with partners in Switzerland. The artistic dial and guilloché work are carried out by independent artisans and long-time ANDERSEN Genève collaborators.

The Celestial Voyager VK Edition is limited to fourteen watches.

About ANDERSEN Genève

Since 1980, ANDERSEN Genève has been creating high-end timepieces for collectors around the world, combining incredible ingenuity with beautiful craftsmanship. Nearly all is produced in limited-edition series or on a bespoke basis for clients seeking something personalised or completely unique. Svend Andersen first achieved fame in the watch world in 1969 with his “Bottle Clock”, a horological take on the ship-in-a-bottle that earned him the nickname “The Watchmaker of the Impossible”, before honing his craft over nine years in the Grand Complications atelier at Patek Philippe. In 1980 he began taking private commissions and soon opened his own Geneva workshop — and ANDERSEN Genève was born.

The firm has since become renowned for its magnificent Worldtime editions; the ingenious “Montre à Tact” (1996), which replaces dial and hands with time-reading windows; its perpetual calendars; and its exceptional Jumping Hour models. Svend Andersen is also co-founder of the Académie Horlogère des Créateurs Indépendants (AHCI), which represents the world’s finest independent watchmakers.

Since 2015, ANDERSEN Genève has been owned and directed by Pierre-Alexandre Aeschlimann, working in close collaboration with Svend Andersen (84 years old), Marco Poluzzi (84 years old), and a small, in-house team of talented watchmakers. Operating from its original workshop overlooking the Rhône in the historic Saint Gervais area of Geneva – once home to the city’s famed cabinotiers watchmakers – and since 2022 with a second Atelier for case-making in La Chaux-de-Fonds, ANDERSEN Genève creates around 50 watches per year, each one a rare and lasting work of art. In fact, fewer than 1,500 timepieces have been manufactured since 1980.

watches.desc:
Audemars Piguet is proud to present the Atelier des Établisseurs, a new way for the company to create remarkable watches honouring collaboration and rare traditional crafts. By producing timepieces in very limited quantities, this new project preserves artisanal skills, while shedding light on the collaborative spirit that has driven the watchmaking industry for generations. The Atelier des Établisseurs builds on the établissage system, a work organisation in place since the end of the 18th century from which Audemars Piguet was born. This concept comes to life with the launch of three exceptional creations that draw on the talent of artisans from diverse backgrounds and combine traditional savoir-faire, modern technology and avant-garde design.

Établisseurs Nomade, pays tribute to watches designed to be used in a variety of ways. Whether slipped in the pocket or placed on the table, this creation combines facetted metal (titanium) and meticulously selected natural stones (black onyx and meteorite). Stones are fragile and require delicate craftsmanship to obtain the desired shape. The lapidarist saws, refines and polishes them slowly until they fit perfectly. The watch offers three positions: closed, open or desk clock. It comes with a specially designed chain in titanium. Calibre 7501 is the true hero of the timepiece. Based on the extra-thin Calibre 7121, which was launched in 2022, it is skeletonised using a hacksaw – a traditional fine handsaw. Playing on transparency and symmetry, the movement is punctuated with bridges that act as hour-markers to indicate the passage of time. Hand-skeletonisation is an exacting skill that only a few watchmakers have mastered. This know-how, which requires precision and patience, particularly when polishing the angles by hand, has been preserved at Audemars Piguet since the 1930s. The outer dial is made of meteorite stone and slips into an architectural case made of a bevelled metal mesh and facetted stones.

Edouard Bovet’s journey to China in 1818 marked the beginning of one of Swiss watchmaking’s most remarkable stories. Born in Fleurier to a watchmaking family and trained in sales in London, he arrived in Guangzhou with four pocket watches, selling them almost immediately, and he went on to establish BOVET as a benchmark of Swiss horology in China. This timepiece distills that voyage into a miniature work of art.

The front dial depicts the tall ship The Orville in hand-executed miniature painting, enhanced with bright Super‑LumiNova that reveals the scene at night. The waves and the sun are hand‑engraved in 18K red gold, while the entire case, bow, attachments, and buckle are decorated with BOVET’s signature Fleurisanne engraving, requiring approximately 130 hours of work. On the reverse side, an off‑set dial crafted from actual stone from the Château de Môtiers reveals the in‑house movement, including BOVET’s own hairspring and regulating organ. The stone is quite fragile, so for every completed dial, six others end up broken on the workshop floor.

The Monsieur Bovet is in the Amadeo system, so it is four timepieces in one – able to be worn on both sides, used as a table clock, or as a pocket timepiece with the provided chain.

A distillation of Edouard Bovet’s trip to China, this timepiece honors the legacy of the 204-year old House of BOVET, which put the village of Fleurier on the watchmaking map. The Monsieur Bovet Tribute to Edouard Bovet is a masterpiece of the skills that owner Pascal Raffy has worked tirelessly to keep alive.s.
